abstract: Can vision-language models turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action? This requires inferring object geometry, anticipating the effects of rotation, and refining actions through visual feedback. We introduce RoTA-Bench to evaluate these abilities through interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Given a target silhouette, a model observes a rotated object and chooses successive rotations to recover the target projection within a limited action budget. Our automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects from 2D icons and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Empirically, we find that (i) a substantial human-model gap persists: GPT-5.6-Sol succeeds on only 17\% of tasks, whereas 20 undergraduate participants collectively complete the test set four times with a 100\% success rate; (ii) image-space and pose-space progress can diverge: at matched states, the model more often improves silhouette overlap while worsening pose alignment than humans (19.4\% vs. 10.9\%); and (iii) fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history: removing it leaves 96.8\% of the model's actions at a coarse 30-degree step size and sharply reduces observed task success. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control, beyond recognizing or matching individual images.
introduction:
Psychological and cognitive-science research establishes spatial perception as a foundational domain of cognitive ability \citep{Carroll_1993}, essential for maintaining object constancy across viewpoints \citep{shepard1971mental} and recovering three-dimensional geometry from two-dimensional projections \citep{richards1987inferring} through the mental representation, manipulation, and inference of shape and orientation. As vision-language models are increasingly applied in visual question answering, interactive agents, and embodied systems \citep{chen2024spatialvlm,wang2026d3d}, agents in interactive settings such as embodied exploration and geometry-aware navigation must translate spatial understanding into physical actions \citep{zhu2025move}. However, current models continue to face challenges in reasoning about three-dimensional positions, orientations, and spatial relationships \citep{ma2025spatialllm}. Therefore, addressing these challenges requires evaluation tools that assess whether models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action.

However, current visual and spatial benchmarks fall short of this requirement. Static benchmarks evaluate spatial reasoning through passive question answering on fixed images \citep{johnson2017clevr,hudson2019gqa,yue2024mmmu,lu2024mathvista}, lacking action execution and closed-loop feedback entirely. Conversely, existing interactive benchmarks spanning software interfaces, visual mazes, and sliding puzzles \citep{zhou2024webarena,xie2024osworld,rodriguezsalgado2026mazebench,mayer2025ivispar} focus on high-level task planning, tool invocation, or spatial pathfinding in complex environments. In these settings, task success largely depends on coding ability, reasoning, and planning, rather than perceiving three-dimensional orientation from visual cues and translating it into action.

To bridge this gap, inspired by classical insights on inferring three-dimensional shape from two-dimensional projections and silhouettes \citep{richards1987inferring}, we ask whether vision-language models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action. Therefore, we introduce RoTA-Bench, an automatically constructed benchmark of interactive 3D-to-2D projection alignment. Our pipeline constructs three-dimensional objects from two-dimensional icons, generates initial orientations through reversible rotations, and guarantees solvability automatically. Given a target silhouette and visual observations of the rotated object, the model selects a rotation from 24 discrete actions at each step, receives an updated observation at the next step, and iteratively refines alignment within a limited action budget. The benchmark contains 674 tasks, with a stratified 100-task test set.
setup:
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate nine vision-language models---GPT-5.6-Sol, GPT-5.6-Terra, GPT-5.6-Luna \citep{openai2026gpt56systemcard}, Gemini 3.6 Flash \citep{google2026gemini36flash}, Claude Opus 5, Claude Sonnet 5 \citep{anthropic2026claudeopus5,anthropic2026claudesonnet5}, Qwen 3.7 Plus \citep{qwen37}, GPT-6-Astra \citep{openai2026gpt6systemcard}, and SpatioLM-Understanding-InternVL3.5 \citep{wu2026spatiolm}---as well as two GPT-5.6-Sol-based agent frameworks, ReAct \citep{yao2022react} and Magentic \citep{fourney2024magentic}, 20 undergraduate participants (Human; Appendix~\ref{app:human-evaluation}), two stochastic baselines (Uniform random and Random with IoU rollback), and two greedy baselines. All evaluations follow a common task protocol, action space, decision budget, success criterion, and termination rules. All models are evaluated at temperature 0; closed-source models are queried via APIs (total cost: \$1,482.07), while SpatioLM is deployed locally on a server equipped with eight NVIDIA A100 (40GB) GPUs. Complete prompts, hyperparameters, agent tools, and evaluation settings are detailed in Appendices~\ref{app:implementation} and~\ref{app:prompts}.
main:
\label{sec:results-main}

Table~\ref{tab:formal-results} presents alignment performance across 100 test tasks, with success counts and confidence intervals in Appendix~\ref{app:success-intervals}. Frontier models struggle markedly on interactive 3D projection alignment: GPT-5.6-Sol achieves the highest success rate at only 17.0\%, followed by Gemini 3.6 Flash at 10.0\%, while ReAct attains the highest final IoU of 0.628 (16.0\% success). Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5, and Qwen 3.7 Plus fail entirely (0.0\% success), with final IoU values (0.484--0.504) barely exceeding uniform random exploration (0.473). Notably, SpatioLM-Understanding-InternVL3.5 suffers a catastrophic policy collapse, where 91.12\% of its actions degenerate into \texttt{YAW\_POS 10$^\circ$}, yielding 0.0\% success and the lowest final IoU of 0.463 (below random actions). In stark contrast, human participants achieve a 100.0\% success rate, reaching an average final IoU of 0.923 in 16.22 steps. As shown in Figure~\ref{fig:mean-iou-main}, human trajectories exhibit overall IoU gains surpassing the 0.90 threshold, whereas model trajectories plateau early between 0.50 and 0.63. The two greedy baselines sharpen this distinction: at each step, each enumerates all 24 legal rotation successors using the ground-truth simulator, then selects the action that maximizes successor projection IoU or minimizes true 3D pose error, respectively. The IoU-greedy baseline succeeds on only 39.0\% of tasks (final IoU 0.725), showing that greedily maximizing immediate projection overlap is insufficient on many tasks; by contrast, the pose-greedy baseline solves every task (100.0\%, final IoU 0.924 in 8.32 steps), showing that reliable access to the true 3D pose error is sufficient to complete all of them. Overall, the success rates and IoU trajectories show a substantial human--model gap on RoTA-Bench.
diagnosis:
\label{sec:results-failures}

We first evaluate whether model failure stems from inadequate visual exploration. As reported in Table~\ref{tab:formal-results}, GPT-5.6-Sol achieves a cumulative surface coverage of 79.58\%, closely trailing human participants (83.07\%), while ReAct (79.08\%) and GPT-6-Astra (78.93\%) maintain comparable exposure. Total coverage is similar, but the regions viewed and their use may differ.

To diagnose model action failures, we decouple each rotation into direction (rotation axis and sign) and angle (step size), which correspond to estimating the direction and magnitude of the 3D pose difference between the current pose and target pose. Evaluating these decomposed components in Table~\ref{tab:formal-results} reveals clear deficiencies on both fronts:
For directional choice, GPT-5.6-Sol selects effective rotation directions far less often than humans (58.75\% vs.\ 83.91\%) and performs only marginally better than uniform random sampling (53.78\%), with other frontier models exhibiting similarly low rates (52.40\%--61.87\%). 
For angular precision, conditioned on choosing an effective direction, GPT-5.6-Sol exhibits a larger mean deviation between its selected angle and the best legal angle (6.49$^\circ$ vs.\ 2.99$^\circ$ for humans; best legal angle rate 61.80\% vs.\ 71.82\%), incurring an average geometric angle loss of 2.25$^\circ$ per step (more than double the 0.96$^\circ$ loss of humans). 
Appendix~\ref{app:finding-one} reports paired confidence intervals for the Human--Sol differences in Effective Direction Rate and Angle Gap. Together, these action metrics show that the human--model gap also appears in rotation direction and angle selection.
conclusion:
\label{sec:conclusion}

RoTA-Bench evaluates whether vision-language models can turn 2D observations into 3D understanding that supports precise action through interactive projection alignment. Its automated pipeline constructs silhouette-preserving 3D objects and uses reversible initialization to guarantee solvability, yielding 674 tasks and a stratified 100-task test set. Evaluations reveal a substantial human--model success gap, show that image-space and pose-space progress can diverge, and find that fine-grained control is sensitive to interaction history. These findings highlight the challenge of converting visual evidence into precise 3D control.
